The overall respiration equation uses one glucose and six oxygen molecules to produce six carbon dioxide molecules, six water molecules, and approximately 30-32 ATP.

Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol without requiring oxygen; it uses one six-carbon glucose, two NAD+, two ATP, and four ADP and produces two three-carbon pyruvate, two NADH, four ATP, and two water molecules, for a net yield of two ATP.
Pyruvate oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and converts two pyruvate into two acetyl-CoA while producing two NADH and two carbon dioxide molecules.

The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and indirectly requires oxygen; two turns use two acetyl-CoA, six NAD+, two FAD, two ADP or GDP, and two four-carbon oxaloacetate and produce four carbon dioxide, six NADH, two FADH2, and two ATP or GTP.

The electron transport chain operates in the inner mitochondrial membrane and cristae; complexes I-IV establish a proton gradient in the intermembrane space, ATP synthase uses that gradient, and oxygen is the final electron acceptor forming water.

Oxidative phosphorylation uses ten NADH, two FADH2, and approximately 26-28 ADP plus phosphate, recycles ten NAD+ and two FAD, and yields approximately 26-28 ATP, with some textbooks reportedly citing 32-34 ATP.
